content.thinking:
I'm picturing a gray wolf in Blizzard/Warcraft style: chunky heroic proportions, oversized paws and head, hand-painted shading with saturated colors, worn leather trim and rivets, standing alert as if geared for war.

I'll add a tattered leather collar with a small fang pendant, keeping accessories minimal so the wolf stays wild rather than domesticated. Scaling it up to heroic size—around 0.85-0.9m shoulder height, stylized chunky proportions beyond real wolf anatomy.

Now I'm planning the skeleton: hips as root joint, with a spine chain running from hips up through the chest to the shoulders, defining joint positions and names along that path since I need to build this carefully without being able to test the API as I go.

I'm sketching out the neck and head placement—raising the neck forward and up for an alert wolf pose, with the head positioned and angled slightly downward, then figuring out how the chain's final joint connects as the parent for the head joint.

For head orientation, it's safer to use local direction words like forward/up/right rather than raw dir vectors, so I'll define the head joint using head.local with forward and up weights for a natural aim.

I'm settling on a convention where "left" corresponds to +X, matching the sign pattern used for side mirroring (s=1 for left), to keep everything consistent across joints. Though honestly, to minimize risk it might be simpler to just stick with plain model-space coordinate literals instead of these word-based conventions.

Since literal points lack bone info, I need to always pass an explicit `bone:` parameter for head parts to avoid ambiguity between head and neck. Now I'm starting to sketch out model-space dimensions for a stylized heroic wolf — shoulder height around 0.85, deep chest, big shoulder mass, with body proportions based on real wolf anatomy.

I'm settling on withers at 0.92m including the shoulder hump, nose tip around 1.0m, ears topping out at 1.18m, for an alert standing pose. Now I'm working through how the body loft should be structured along the spine — figuring out which joints own which path segments when hips and spine1 start at the same point, since overlapping ownership could cause the hips joint to get dropped.

For the overall skeleton, I'm settling on a root "hips" joint at the pelvis, with a "spine" chain running forward and a "tail" chain running backward, both parented to hips and sliced from the same body path in opposite directions — mirroring the doc's root/front/back chain pattern.

The round cap extends past the loft start by the pelvis width radius, so hips at z=-0.5 gets a bit of extra coverage even though both hips and spine1 resolve to t≈0 at that point. Since the last-listed bone wins ties, spine1 ends up owning that vertex region while hips gets dropped, meaning hips contributes nothing directly to the body mesh.

Now I'm planning the hind legs, parented to hips, with hip joints at x=±0.13, y=0.7, z=-0.5. For digitigrade wolf legs I'm laying out the chain as thigh (femur) angling forward-down, stifle (knee) forward, hock back, then a vertical metatarsus leading to the paw, with segment lengths around 0.30/0.30/0.24 before the flat toes meet the floor.

I'm second-guessing the sole/bends interaction — the docs seem inconsistent about whether sole reduces the number of required bend directions by one, since the bird example uses 3 bends with 4 segments plus a sole. To avoid risking a parameter-count error, I'll just skip the sole option and use a simpler 3-segment limb (thigh, shin, metatarsus) with 2 bend directions.

For the foot I'll build it as a separate chunky part attached at the end joint, placing the ankle target and checking the fold geometry works out with lengths 0.32/0.32/0.26 against the vertical drop, then setting bends for the two inner joints and naming the limb segments accordingly.

I decide 4 names with a tip joint: ["hipL","kneeL","hockL","pawL"], so paw geometry sits on the tip aimed along the end tangent. I'm also considering adding toe joints as digit roles for the rig, planning a small chain of toe joints per paw within the 160-joint budget.

Then for front legs, I'm sketching shoulder → elbow → carpus → paw structure based on real dog anatomy (scapula, humerus, forearm, carpus), setting shoulder joint positions and keeping limbs extended in a standing neutral pose for rest.

With the last segment held vertical, the first two at 0.32 each give about a 38° elbow bend, which looks moderate and natural. I'll keep the limbs thick for a heroic proportion.

Now for the hind leg: with hip at 0.72 and ankle target at 0.13, the thigh folds sharply at roughly 71° from vertical to cover the shortened reach, pushing the knee forward about 0.27 and bringing the shin back toward the hock by a similar amount.

I'll set the paw target slightly behind the hip horizontally to get that natural wolf-like hock bend, letting the two-bone IK work out the hip-to-hock distance from there since the solver handles the final segment orientation automatically.

Checking the metatarsus and paw placement, the hock ends up around y=0.39, with the oversized paw geometry (an ellipsoid roughly 0.075 by 0.06 by 0.11) sitting chunky and forward to match the stylized proportions.

For the toes, I'm adding three small claw bumps up front with cone-shaped claws in a dark bone color, using a spike helper for the claw geometry.

Now I'm laying out the body loft stations from rump to chest, defining the width, height, and vertical center positions at each cross-section to build that heroic deep-chested, tucked-waist silhouette.

Lowering the chest station center to around y=0.70 with height .48 so the bottom lands near 0.46, aligning with where the elbow should sit on the dog's body relative to the legs reaching down to the ground at 0.13.

Still working out body stations...

Continuing to [0,1.02,0.72], rising forward for an alert posture with the head carried high. Neck tapers from radius 0.15 to 0.12 with a thick ruff, parented to the third spine joint. The skull sits around [0,1.03,0.80] with the muzzle extending forward to z≈1.12, giving a total nose-to-tail length of about 2.2m including the tail.

Now I'm orienting the head to aim slightly forward and down, keeping the axis simple at roughly [0,-0.08,1]. I'm detailing head components: a scaled sphere for the skull with gradient fur paint, a brow ridge for a heroic/angry look, and glowing amber eyes built from a small sphere with a dark slit pupil plus an eyelid wedge.

Still defining eye geometry...

Adding a jaw joint with its own sweep for the mouth, keeping it closed at rest but letting white fang cones peek out for an alert snarl, plus a thin dark lip line tracing the mouth corner.

Now I'm positioning the nose pad as a small dark rounded sphere with faint nostril bumps in near-black tones, then moving to the ears -- large erect triangular extrusions set near the top-back of the skull to fit the oversized Warcraft-style proportions.

I should keep x and y orthogonal to avoid skewing the ear shape, so I'll set x along one axis and y with the backward lean on a perpendicular axis, handling outward lean separately.

Working out the ear outline points for width and height...

Working out the inner ear detail with a smaller offset extrude positioned forward using the cross product of the local axes to find the correct outward direction for both mirrored sides.

Figuring out positioning logic...

Now I'm thinking about adding shaggy fur details — cheek ruffs, neck ruff, and chest mane cards — since that shagginess is a signature Warcraft wolf trait. I plan to draw these as grayscale fur-tuft SVG cards so the coat's color paint can tint them appropriately.

Writing SVG tuft shape...

Now I'm figuring out fur card scattering: around 500-800 cards per body, keeping triangle counts cheap, filtering placement by surface normal so fur doesn't appear on the belly, and letting the cards flow naturally with gravity so they're seen edge-on from the side.

I'm adding separate scatter passes for the neck ruff and chest mane, with larger cards and tighter minimum spacing to build denser tufts in those areas.

Now I'm chaining a bushy tail from the hips with a slightly curving downward path, defining joint positions that sweep back and down to give it a relaxed hanging pose.

Writing tail radius and color logic...

Checking the tail stays above ground level, then I move to the hind-leg structure, thinking through a separate thigh bulge sweep with its own radius profile and blending it smoothly along the chain by position rather than per-segment.

I'm tapering the thigh-to-paw radius array across knee, shin, and hock, with the hock needing a small spherical bump to read as a sharp joint and the thigh needing its own bulge to feel muscular.

For the haunch I'm adding a separate ellipsoid for the thigh muscle attached at the hip joint, then building the shoulder mass as an oversized scapula ellipsoid with an elbow sphere, and defining a tapering radius profile for the front leg ending in a chunky paw.

Now I'm checking foot placement against ground contact for both front and hind paws, computing the distance from hip root to hind target to verify the leg segment lengths sum correctly, and confirming the hind limb bends within the correct YZ plane before setting up the front leg's root and target positions.

The elbow sits slightly buried in the body, which is anatomically correct for a canine. I'm parenting the front legs to spine3 near its tail end, and deciding joint naming conventions like shoulderL/elbowL/carpusL/pawFL so auto-riggers recognize the chain properly.

Settling on consistent naming: front legs use shoulderL/elbowL/wristL/pawFL, hind legs use hipL/kneeL/hockL/pawHL, both tagged with role "leg" and four joints forming three spans plus a tip. For toes I'm adding digit joints parented to each paw, positioned slightly forward and aimed outward, with each paw getting a main pad bump plus three toe nubs and several claws.

Now I'm picking a hand-painted Warcraft-style wolf palette—cool slate-blue grays for the base fur, a deep blue-gray for the saddle/back, lighter gray-blue highlights, and a warm cream tone for the underbelly.

Rounding out the palette with warm ochre-brown accents for legs/cheeks/ears, dark shadow tones, a near-black nose, and a glowing amber eye color. For gear, I'm settling on leather browns, bronze/brass rivets, bone-white fang details, and steel accents—planning a riveted leather collar with a bone fang pendant and a chest strap with a small metal ring for that worn, hand-painted detail look.

Still deciding on tribal war-paint marks—thinking a small decal of red claw-slash stripes on the shoulder blade, positioning it with a direction vector so it faces outward on whichever flank I'm working on, mirroring the orientation for the opposite side.

For the actual coat paint, I'm moving past cel-shading toward a more hand-painted Blizzard look: blending countershading (darker back, cream belly) with normal-based gradient lighting and some brush-stroke noise mottling to break up flat color.

Writing coat paint function...

Still writing fur grain layers...

Actually that's wrong since leg fur runs vertically, so I need a separate grain paint with axis "y" for the legs instead. I'm also thinking about adding a subtle painted shadow gradient for a hand-painted look, plus warm tan-ochre accents on the lower legs like real gray wolves have, possibly with darker front leg stripes.

Writing gradient paint logic...

Now I'm moving to the head paint, blending a cream muzzle and cheeks with a darker stripe over the nose bridge and dark ears, using a countershading sweep between the muzzle top and sides.

For the skull and forehead I'm applying a similar countershading paint, skipping extra nose decals to keep things simple. I'm placing thin whisker rods on each side of the muzzle, three per side, pale off-white, and starting to lay out the upper fang teeth.

For the fangs, I'm angling upper canines downward and lower ones upward so they peek out along the closed lip line, colored in a pale ivory tone, and skipping the gums and tongue since the mouth stays shut. Now I'm thinking through the eye assembly—glowing amber iris, pupil, and lid—plus considering adding a crest of dark mane spikes along the spine, though I need to figure out how to trace a path along the body's dorsal line since the body itself is built from a loft.

For the mane spikes, I'm working out whether to orient each spike along the sweep path's tangent or along the surface normal, since tangent-aligned spikes would lie flat along the back leaning forward rather than standing up and leaning back the way I want—so I'm computing tip positions manually by offsetting outward along the normal plus a backward tilt.

I'm planning dorsal spikes running from mid-body to tail and a second row along the neck, keeping them small with low-poly detail for a heroic silhouette feel, and considering whether a darker crest color with lighter tips would read well on cone geometry.

Now I'm adding smaller fur details: jagged cheek ruffs angled backward in pale cream tones, shoulder tufts, and spurs at the elbow and hock joints, each anchored to specific bone positions pulled from the limb point arrays. For the paws, I'm planning dark claw cones angled forward-down on the toes, accounting for the visible front toes versus the fanned rear ones.

Then I'm shifting to the collar, building it as a surface loop swept around the neck, working out how to orient the cutting plane given the neck's thirty-degree tilt so the loop wraps cleanly rather than cutting obliquely or blending into the body mesh.

I'm uncertain about the section radius orientation for the collar band—whether rx/ry align with the tube axis or the binormal—and considering just using a simple circular cross-section instead to avoid getting a mis-oriented thick radial band.

Now I'm adding brass studs along the collar loop using spheres placed at frame points from the path, confirming that stud orientation doesn't matter since they're spherical. I'm positioning the whole collar slightly below the main sweep geometry.

For the pendant, I need to find the underside point of the neck sweep (angle 180, the belly side) and hang a cord with a fang spike pointing downward from there, roughly centered below the chest.

Checking the pendant's position against the chest sphere, I realize it would actually be buried inside the body at that spot, so I'm shifting it forward along the neck curve to a point further out where the underside sits clear of the chest geometry.

Now thinking about the neck itself: it needs to end before the skull starts, with the collar placed along the neck rather than on the head, and the neck radius should be sized comparably to the head width to give that wolf-like ruffed appearance. I'm also setting up the neck as a two-segment chain ("neck1", "neck2") so it can be smoothly skinned along its sweep.

Next I'm defining the jaw joint attached to the head, with its position and aim vectors placed near the mouth area, and sketching the lower jaw as a tapered sweep rigged to that single jaw bone, with cream-gray shading for the chin and lower jaw region.

Then I'm shaping the upper muzzle as another tapered sweep bound to the head bone, and adding thin dark lip-line sweeps running from the nose back to the mouth corners on each side, checking that the muzzle's curvature lines up properly with where the lip line sits.

For the lip line itself I'll use small dark points roughly radius .007 to suggest a thread-like seam. For the fangs, I'm placing the upper pair near the jaw tip pointing downward, but checking they clear the lower jaw's top surface so they don't intersect it, adjusting the spike length and position accordingly.

Working out that lower fangs would end up hidden inside the muzzle geometry, so I'll skip those and only add the upper fangs, along with slightly posing the jaw open for a parted-mouth look.

Now I'm positioning the eyes against the skull sphere, working out the offset coordinates so they sit correctly on the curved surface using the radii and height factors.

Building the eyeball layers...

I'll skip the eyeliner rim detail and instead add a brow fur tuft spike sweeping from above the eye forward, plus a small pale eyebrow spot like real wolves have, positioned with cream color above each eye.

For the nose, I'm placing the nose pad sphere with its scale and two small black nostril ellipsoids, plus a tiny specular highlight dot on top for a painted Warcraft-style look, along with a darker muzzle bridge stripe. I'm also planning cheek ruff spikes and a downward-pointing chin tuft spike at the jaw.

I'm scattering small fur cards across the skull for a fuzzy look, then working through the body loft code using station arrays with bone references tied to hips and spine joints -- confirming that hips works as the root joint and that the tail chain parents to hips. I'm also checking how the spine, neck, and chest sections connect in z-position, with the neck sweep picking up the coat color.

Now I'm defining a cream chest bib patch using a custom paint mask with a zigzag edge based on position and normal thresholds, and extending that cream coloring up under the neck as well.

I'll define my own zigzag function to avoid the extra dependency, then write a shading helper that darkens or lightens a base color based on surface normal, using resolve and mix to blend the tones smoothly.

Adding ambient occlusion near the ground and joints, pulling in the proper types for color and paint, and checking texture resolution math to make sure the shared paint sheet gives enough detail per square meter of fur.

I'm bumping paint resolution up for crisper grain, confirming the triangle budget stays comfortable with cards and sweeps, and now sketching out gear ideas — a leather collar with brass studs and pendant, a shoulder war-paint decal, maybe a bracer strap or a bone-bead braid hanging from the neck.

I'm leaning toward a spiked brass collar instead, placing spikes radially around the neck loop by sampling points along the sweep's path with outward-facing normals so each spike inherits the correct orientation and weighting.

Still building the collar sweep...

For the pendant, I'm reconsidering replacing it with a bronze ring and fang hanging from the neck's front-bottom, rather than keeping the original tooth-on-cord design — using a small torus plus a downward spike at the collar center point.

I'm checking whether this placement actually clears the chest sphere geometrically; computing the position shows it falls inside the chest ellipsoid, so it would be buried unless I offset it forward and down, or raise the collar higher on the neck instead.

Trying t=.75 now puts the pendant clearly outside the chest shape, but creates a new problem: the collar sits too close to the back of the skull near the cheek ruff, which would get hidden. I need to find a middle position, maybe around t=.62, that clears both the chest and the skull.

Lowering the pendant slightly forward so it clears the chest fur cards, then shifting to foreleg bracers — I'm sketching cuffs around the forearm using ring points swept along the leg chain with a closed catmull curve.

I decide to only add leather bracers to the front legs, skipping the hind legs or hocks for simplicity, plus brass rivet studs for detail. Now I'm drawing war-paint claw slashes as an SVG decal on the shoulder, three diagonal red-orange gashes with darker edges...

For placement, I'm positioning the decal near the scapula ellipsoid's surface, checking that the coordinates line up with the shoulder mass and chest geometry so it reads naturally on the body.

I'm leaving decal color unset since the paint is positional, which keeps shoulder shading seamless with the rest of the body. I'm attaching the scapula bone to the shoulder joint of the leg chain so it moves correctly, then setting up a loop over both left/right sides to generate these parts symmetrically.

Now I'm setting up the imports, metadata, and color palette for the wolf model...

Writing paint helper logic...

I'm switching to a warm highlight tone for that hand-painted Warcraft look, then setting up grain-based paint functions for the back fur, side fur, and belly fur, each with distinct colors and seeds.

Now I'm layering these with countershade blending, which gradually transitions from back coloring on top-facing surfaces toward belly coloring on bottom-facing ones using a smooth falloff curve. I'm also considering adding mottle blending on the sides to introduce darker blotch patterns for more natural variation.

Moving to the body coat, I'm painting it with the combined coat function and adding cream coloring on the chest and neck for the underside. For the legs, I'm working out a gradient between side fur and tan tones running vertically, plus trying to add a dark stripe down the front of the forelegs to mimic real wolf coloring, based on surface normal and position checks.

Still figuring out the dark leg stripe boundary and zigzag edge, then moving on to head and skull coloring with countershading between back fur tones and a cream muzzle/cheek area.

For the skull, I'm defining cheek patches with cream fur and zigzag edges against a grayer base tone, and now moving to ear coloring with a darker grainy outer layer and a pinkish-brown inner ear tone.

I'm confirming the flat-color paint helper still works fine even though the head sits above the ground shading threshold, since normal-based lighting will still make it read correctly. Now I'm setting up the gradient paint for the tail.

Still writing body loft and spine chain setup...

Checking the tail placement relative to the rump and hips, that looks right. For the neck I'm building a two-span catmull chain running up to the base of the skull, and now I'm placing the head joint and reconsidering where the skull center should actually sit given the neck's endpoint.

To keep things consistent, I'm defining a small helper that expresses all head geometry (skull center, eyes, muzzle) as offsets relative to the head pivot rather than absolute coordinates, so the whole head frame stays coherent even with the slight downward tilt. Writing head geometry offsets...

Checking the total head length though, from skull back to nose tip it comes out around 0.46m, which is way too long for a wolf head proportionally, so I need to shorten the muzzle extent to bring it back toward a believable size.

Now I'm working out the jaw geometry, placing the pivot joint and sweeping it forward so the jaw tip sits just inside the muzzle's underside when closed, with the back of the jaw sized to taper naturally into the skull.

Checking the fang placement next, positioning base and tip coordinates so they sit just outside the jaw's edge and extend down alongside it without poking through the jaw's bottom.

Then I'm working out the lip line points along the muzzle, tracing coordinates from the snout tip back toward the corner of the mouth, checking each against the muzzle's cross-sectional radius to make sure the line stays on the lower surface rather than floating outside it.

Now I'm placing the ears, computing the skull surface at the base point using the ellipsoid equation to check it's roughly on the surface, then nudging it slightly inward since the sum came out just over 1. I'm also figuring the ear height and projecting the tip position upward from the base.

Rethinking ear proportions for a heroic wolf design—scaling up from typical wolf ear ratios to about 0.16m tall with a 0.10m base, and sketching an outline with a sharp tip point. I'm computing the absolute tip height relative to the head top, then working out the orientation vector so the ears lean upright with a slight forward tilt rather than backward, deriving the orthogonal basis vectors for that tilted ear axis.

I verify the cross product sign flips correctly between left and right ears to confirm forward-facing normals, then briefly consider adding small cream fur tufts along the inner ear rim but decide to skip that detail.

Next I'm sketching cheek ruff spikes, positioning their base coordinates symmetrically outward using the side sign, then computing matching tip offsets to make the spikes sweep back and outward in cream coloring.

Now I'm starting the actual builder code -- defining the model, setting up the random seed, and placing the first spine joint for the hips, debating whether to assign a role to the root joint.

Writing leg-building loop...

I'm weighing whether to switch the limb path to catmull for smoother silhouettes rather than sharp polyline joints, since the joint positions stay exact as knots while the curve rounds between them.

Tweaking the front leg's sweep radii at each keyframe to get a chunkier, heroic taper from shoulder to wrist...

Now I'm sketching helpers for a small elbow spike, deciding to skip a wrist pad, and starting a buildPaw function that places sphere geometry at the paw joints to form rounded toes.

Writing paw and toe geometry...

Setting toe joints with digit role for each paw, checking position overlaps between paw and ankle to make sure the geometry covers front and hind legs properly, with the hind legs needing digitigrade posture where the metatarsus stays elevated off the ground.

Now I'm working out the hind leg haunch geometry and bend math, placing the hip sphere and computing bone chain lengths with trigonometry to find where the hock and knee joints should sit given the target foot position.

Solving for the knee position using the perpendicular offset formula, I get it landing around y .45, z -.29, which puts it just under the belly—roughly matching where a real wolf's stifle sits beneath the flank, so this checks out against the thigh length of .32.

I'm noting the thigh radius of .11 will likely clip into the body mesh, which I'll need to address.

Now computing the front leg: solving the elbow position between the root and wrist joints using the same triangle-inequality approach (unequal segment lengths of .34 and .32), finding the perpendicular offset toward the back of the body to place the elbow correctly in the bend.

Let me try shorter upper/lower lengths instead, like .30 and .30 with a .14 paw segment, checking if the resulting reach matches the target vertical distance of .67 — the math still doesn't quite close, so I need to keep adjusting the segment ratios.

Adjusting target z to root z plus 0.02 for a near-vertical stance, I check the resulting elbow-to-wrist slant and realize it's forward-leaning rather than straight down, since the wolf's scapula naturally angles the shoulder joint lower and forward, which constrains what IK alone can achieve.

Working through the geometry with humerus head at the shoulder root and ankle target below, I compute the elbow position via the perpendicular offset from the midpoint, getting a forearm that slants forward about 36 degrees because the straight-line distance is noticeably shorter than the sum of the limb segments, forcing that fold.

Trying progressively shorter limb lengths to reduce that fold—from .28/.28 down to .26/.26 and finally .24/.24—I get the slant angle dropping to near zero, matching the near-straight leg I want, so I settle on something close to .25/.25 segments with a mild ~25 degree bend as a reasonable compromise.

I'm also cross-checking the wrist position when the forearm points straight from root to target, confirming the elbow y-position lands right at the chest bottom, and verifying the hip, shoulder, and spine joints all sit at sensible heights relative to the body's muscle ellipsoids.

The haunch ellipsoid near the hips bulges out nicely to match a thigh shape, but the shoulder blade ellipsoid is making the shoulder top slightly too high compared to the withers, so I'm nudging its center and radius down a bit to fix that bump.

Checking that these sphere-based ellipsoids pick up the paint correctly since the geometry has proper UVs for position-based coloring, and the coat texture orientation is fine along the z-axis. Now I'm sketching out a fur tuft texture as an SVG gradient shape, grey-to-white, to use for fur card rendering.

I want a second tuft variant for visual variety, a sharper hair clump with multiple spikes, so I can randomly alternate between the two textures. Then I'm scattering points across the body surface, filtering out points facing downward, and generating fur cards from those hit points using the tuft textures.

I'm also planning a separate scatter for the belly area with filtered downward-facing points, using larger cards and the coat color to simulate longer underside fur.

Now I'm adding more scatters: a neck ruff following the neck sweep, a chest mane filtered by forward-facing normals with a cream bib color, and tail cards following the tail sweep with backward-leaning flow directions.

Legs get 60 cards each on their upper surfaces, filtered to the top portion, totaling around 1360 cards across the whole creature, which works out to roughly 11k triangles once accounting for bend segmentation. The loft body itself stays cheap at around 250 tris with 5 stations and 15 rings.

For the back crest, I'm placing spikes along the body's surface using points sampled at increasing t values, leaning them backward with dark flat coloring, and doing similarly for the neck sweep from t=.1 to .9. Checking that angle 0 on the surface function correctly points toward world-up for spike placement.

Working out spike geometry now—combining a surface base point with offset vectors for lean, and increasing spike height near the shoulders using a sine-based scale. Then considering adding a decal for shoulder claw marks using the target surface and texture parameters.

Placing the shoulder decals symmetrically at matched ellipsoid coordinates, and thinking about adding war-paint-style facial markings under the eyes as another decal.

Placing the cheek stripe decals at the correct skull surface coordinates...

Now I'm thinking through the eye glow effect using the glow helper with flat pupil color, and scattering decorative skull cards across the surface while filtering out positions that would overlap the eyes or ears.

Writing muzzle whisker rods...

Now I'm placing the brow spikes above each eye with dark coloring, plus a small bright cream accent spot positioned just outside the skull surface near the brow.

Working through the eye sphere depth, I find it protrudes slightly too much, so I adjust the eye center x-position to .082 for a better .015 bulge. Then I move to defining the eye's outward-forward direction vector and placing the pupil as a vertical slit ellipsoid slightly offset toward the front.

Now I'm switching to a round pupil instead: a small black sphere plus a tiny white highlight sphere offset upward and inward for shine. Adding an eyelid sphere flattened and tilted, plus a darker liner ellipsoid positioned behind the eyeball to create a subtle ring around the amber iris, confirming the layering looks right with the liner peeking through thinly.

Now I'm adding leather bracers on the forelegs using a closed swept tube around the leg, with brass rivets placed at the front-facing angle plus a couple offset to the sides, embedding small spheres into the leather surface.

I'm placing a cuff around the forearm, with the wrist and elbow positions calculated from the leg's total length so the cuff lands mid-forearm, giving it a worn Warcraft-style trim with rivets, and considering whether to add a similar cuff detail near the hock on the hind leg.

Thinking further, I decide against extra straps or a girth band to avoid over-engineering the design, but like the idea of a storytelling touch: a couple of feather cards hanging from the collar's left side, using tinted feather SVG textures with their own gradient colors, sized and angled to hang naturally, and I'm weighing whether to use two or three feathers in different colors.

I'll use frame() to anchor two feather cards—one red, one teal—at the collar's side attach point, hanging straight down over the ruff with a 180-degree lean so they drape vertically from the neck.

For the feather bundle itself, I'm checking whether the attach point clears the chest and shoulder geometry, then considering spreading three cards at slightly different angles so they don't stack perfectly on top of each other.

Writing feather SVG shape...

Checking the card orientation again: the root edge should sit at the top near the collar with the tip hanging downward, which matches the physical placement correctly. I'll skip adding a bead or thong detail since the collar ring already anchors it visually.

For the pendant, I'm adding a small brass torus ring hanging at the neck, oriented to face forward by default. Then I'm placing a fang spike anchored just below it, pointing downward, making sure to bind it explicitly to the correct neck joint so it doesn't attach to the wrong bone.

Now I'm working out the neck sweep with a tapering radius profile, placing 12 collar points around it for leather loops, then adding brass spike cones outward at each point instead of rivets.

Next I'm defining the hind leg spikes: a calcaneus spur jutting backward from the hock joint, and an elbow spike angled downward and back, both derived from the limb's point array with matching gray coat coloring.

For the paws, I'm deciding to keep using the leg's gradient paint so the lower portion naturally reads tan, avoiding a separate dedicated paw color.

I'm using dark claws for contrast, then checking the overall palette stays around twenty flat colors. I'm verifying the legs are properly skinned with the sweep function using that leg paint, and double-checking gaps between the shoulder ellipsoid and body, plus confirming the pose stays neutral throughout.

I'm verifying floor contact — making sure the lowest points like paws and claws sit within tolerance of the ground plane — and then working out the overall height by tracing up through the skull, ears, and their base positions.

Now I'm reconsidering proportions: total height comes out to about 1.31, with the head riding higher than expected since the neck is raised in an alert pose, which actually matches how wolves carry themselves when alert. I'm checking body length too — from rump to nose it's running long at 1.8, mostly because the neck stretches forward significantly beyond the chest, so I'm thinking about whether to adjust the body span and neck angle to bring the proportions closer to a realistic 1.3.

Adding tail length brings total to about 2.1m, close enough to real wolf proportions. I'll set the head pivot at [0,1.05,0.68] and derive the neck chain and collar position relative to it, keeping the pendant placement consistent.

The neck sweep ends inside the skull, so I'm defining the jaw joint parented to the head with its aim pointing down and forward, then rigging a rigid jaw bone along a short path for the mouth sweep. I'll add a chin tuft spike under the jaw for detail and skip the tongue for now, moving on to compute remaining pieces referencing the head pivot.
